# Best practices: engineering rules for every agent on both lab machines

One rule set, consolidated on 2026-11-06 at the operator's request from eight earlier Global memories of the two lab stores (listed under "Sources"). The operator's words are quoted under "Sources" at the end. It applies to all agents on both lab machines, LAB-OMARCHY and PAYTON-LEGION2, and across workspaces.

## 1. Code documentation: every code change

1.1. Every code change carries proper XML documentation that describes the affected code.

1.2. That documentation includes a dated change log entry listing the associated canonical requirement ids and descriptive acceptance-criterion ids, plus what changed and why.

1.3. Maintain purpose, behavior, parameters, returns and exceptions, as applicable.

1.4. Preserve earlier change log entries.

1.5. Verify every id against the canonical workspace records. Do not invent traceability or imply acceptance.

1.6. Where XML documentation is unsupported, use the language's native documentation comments with equivalent dated requirement, acceptance-criterion and change fields.

1.7. This is source documentation, not a request for per-PR release notes or an unrelated retrospective sweep.

1.8. Workspace guidance and examples: AGENTS.md and .cursor/rules/code-documentation-traceability.mdc.

## 2. Test runs: targeted after an edit, full gate set once at phase exit

2.1. After an edit, a BDPv4 mock gate or binding runs only the changed test classes, through the Nuke target TestGroups (TR-MCP-NUKE-020), never raw dotnet test.

2.2. The command: ./build.ps1 TestGroups --test-groups "<test project>:<Class>[,<Class>...]" ["<project>:<Class>..." ...] --test-run-id <run id>

2.3. TestGroups writes one TRX per project under TestResults/<run id>/groups/<project>/<project>.trx.

2.4. It selects the named classes whatever their category, but excludes cases tagged for the other platform (Platform!=Windows on Linux, Platform!=Linux on Windows).

2.5. It fails on an unknown project, a group that selects no case, a named class that ran no case, or any failed or skipped case.

2.6. The full gate set (Nuke Test, MigrationIntegrationTests, Build.Tests and ValidateTraceability, on both hosts) runs once, at the final head, to validate phase exit before hostile validation.

2.7. If a gate then fails: fix it, test the fix through TestGroups, and run the full gate set once more at the new head.

2.8. In McpServer, TestGroups is on branch fix/unit-suite-green-20261019 (PR 87) until that pull request merges into develop.

## 3. Windows paths

3.1. Use forward slashes in Windows paths (for example F:/GitHub/vice-sharp and C:/msys64/usr/bin/bash.exe), including paths handed to MSYS2 tools such as gcc, and in scripts, configs and generated build or link arguments.

## 4. Unit tests and integration tests

4.1. Unit tests and integration tests live in separate projects and are correctly tagged.

4.2. Unit tests exercise code in isolation, using controlled mocks or fakes as needed.

4.3. Any test that depends on the environment is an integration test, and is never classified or run as a unit test.

4.4. Apply this distinction to test-project ownership, category tags, Nuke groups and gates, and reported test evidence, across workspaces.

4.5. Preserve BDPv4's green, discriminating mock gates before production changes.

## 5. Emulators

5.1. When the work that needs an emulator is complete, shut the emulator down to a known state and freeze it.

5.2. Restore it from that frozen state only when active work needs it.

5.3. Never leave an emulator running idle and consuming resources after its work is complete.

## 6. Git worktrees

6.1. Create git worktrees inside the owning repository's workspace directory, never as sibling directories beside it. Example: TruckMate worktrees belong under F:/GitHub/TruckMate/.worktrees/<name>. This applies to every repository.

## 7. NuGet warnings

7.1. NuGet warnings may never be ignored.

7.2. Do not suppress NU1902, NU1903 or any other NuGet warning, downgrade an enforced warning gate, disable NuGet audit, or use a local or bootstrap exception to bypass them.

7.3. Repair the dependency issue within the authorized scope, or report the exact affected dependency and the scope decision it needs.

7.4. The operator explicitly rejected a local-only advisory warning override for the pinned FeatureFlags tool bootstrap.

## 8. Mistakes and accountability

8.1. Acknowledge your mistakes, state the rule you broke, and account for the wasted usage and time.

8.2. State the specific action and its consequence.

8.3. Give measured usage and elapsed time when available, and keep measured facts apart from estimates and unavailable figures.

# HV rules: hostile-validation rules for every agent and every HV round

One rule set, merged on 2026-11-06 from MEMORY-PROCESS-010 (version 2) and MEMORY-PROCESS-013 (version 1), reformatted and refined at the operator's request. The operator's words are quoted under "Sources" at the end. "Task" means one task of the plan under review (in McpServer, one implementation task of the plan's TODO). "Change under review" means the commits or edits the HV round reviews. A requirement is "in flux" when a change under review adds, changes or implements it.

## 1. Verdicts and scores

1.1. Every HV round returns an overall verdict, AGREE or DISAGREE, with an accuracy score and a completeness score. The overall verdict is AGREE only when both scores are 98 or more.

1.2. Every HV round also returns a verdict for each task it adjudicates (rule 3.2): AGREE or DISAGREE, with that task's own accuracy and completeness scores. A task's AGREE needs both of its scores at 98 or more.

1.3. The per-task verdicts are the operator's own gates. They are not extra approval gates added by an agent.

## 2. Marking tasks completed, and regressions

2.1. A task that clears its own HV AGREE is marked completed in the plan and in its TODO, through the agent's plugin. The completion cites that round's request JSONL, its response JSONL and the session-log turn that holds the verdict.

2.2. A task without its own AGREE stays open, whatever the overall verdict.

2.3. A completed task is not adjudicated again as an incomplete task. It is checked only for regression, when rule 3.3 selects it. A regression is any finding that would invalidate a completed task. A task with a regression is reopened, because no done state may stand while a failure is outstanding, and it stays open until a later round clears it again.

2.4. Every regression is called out in the review summary, by task, with the finding and the requirement it touches.

2.5. Per-task verdicts keep each round tied to the plan's tasks, which helps against scope creep.

## 3. Review scope: the requirements matrix

3.1. The reviewer builds and keeps, and returns with its verdict, a matrix of: the requirements of each task, and the requirements of each change under review. The matrix shows which requirements are in flux and which tasks share them.

3.2. An open task with at least one requirement in flux is adjudicated in full and gets its own verdict and scores (rule 1.2).

3.3. A completed task that shares a requirement in flux gets regression attention only (rule 2.3). Its result is either "no regression" or a regression finding.

3.4. A task with no requirement being adjudicated in this round is not reviewed, unless the operator requests a holistic review. This holds for open tasks as well as completed ones: an open task out of scope stays open for that round. For example, an HV midway through a plan, such as a phase gate, still sees requirements and tasks of other phases; they are out of scope for that review. The matrix still lists them, marked out of scope.

## 4. What every HV request contains

4.1. Every task of the plan under review, each with a fixed number and its state (open or completed), and the changes under review.

4.2. The requirement to return the matrix (rule 3.1), a verdict and both scores for each task adjudicated in full (rule 3.2), a regression result for each task selected for regression (rule 3.3), and the regressions called out in the summary (rule 2.4).

4.3. Rule 6 (infrastructure failures), stated explicitly.

4.4. Complete paired request and response JSONL, and the complete verdict artifacts, are kept for every round.

## 5. Interpreting findings

5.1. Reason about the context and the underlying failure pattern of each finding. Do not merely patch the cited line or satisfy the reviewer's wording.

5.2. Understand the affected user outcome and the claim the evidence is meant to support.

5.3. Verify each finding against authoritative sources.

5.4. Examine related instances and the end-to-end chain among requirements, design, implementation, tests, evidence, documentation, publication and actual deployment, as applicable.

5.5. Check whether a proposed fix and its tests address the underlying class of failure without introducing new gaps.

5.6. Keep observed facts apart from inference, unverified claims and unresolved decisions.

5.7. Preserve full review receipts, and report every FAIL and every UNKNOWN.

5.8. Apply the existing plan and review rules. Do not invent additional approval gates, and do not treat passing a replacement check as proof of the user outcome.

## 6. Infrastructure failures

6.1. Infrastructure failures have no bearing on HV AGREE when sufficient review evidence is present. Judge the requested product, plan, requirements, code, tests and retained evidence on their merits.

6.2. MCP availability, live memory-loading failures, triage submission, session-log persistence or readback, and other infrastructure failures must not by themselves force DISAGREE, lower a score or block acceptance when the needed evidence is otherwise available.

6.3. Record infrastructure failures separately, as operational issues. Use the supported failsafe and retry persistence without delaying the substantive verdict.

6.4. If a failure actually prevents access to evidence needed for a specific criterion, name that missing evidence and the affected criterion honestly. Never invent a PASS or an AGREE.

6.5. Rule 6 supersedes older profile or template rules that made infrastructure persistence or live memory loading a prerequisite for HV AGREE.

# Byrd Development Process Utilizing AI

**v4 - TDD Alignment with Fowler**  
**April 2026**  
**Payton Byrd (The Sharp Ninja)**

## Version History

### v4 (2026-04)
- Refined the description of Test-Driven Development in the Implementation and Validation sections to more closely align with Martin Fowler's canonical definition (Red → Green → Refactor cycle, incremental "next small piece of behavior").
- Explicitly positioned the mocks-first validation and full-suite regression gates as *Byrd-specific augmentations* for AI safety rather than core TDD.
- Added language emphasizing refactoring as part of the cycle.
- These changes reduce drift from canonical TDD while preserving the essential AI-risk mitigations that define the Byrd process.
- See docs/plans/TDD-Byrd-vs-Fowler-Analysis.md and docs/plans/Proposed-TDD-Wording-Changes.md for detailed comparison and before/after text.

### v3 and earlier
Original content preserved below, with the v4 TDD refinements applied in the Implementation and Validation sections.

---
## Overview

The major differences between Humans writing code and AI writing code is that Humans are able to link seemingly unrelated concepts into a web of possible solutions for a problem in a truly creative way, but often lack enough experience or knowledge to follow through to completion before encountering unforeseen challenges that create delay and doubt, both of which create distractions that cloud the focus necessary to stay on task and on timeline, both resulting in increased expense and opportunity loss.

AI brings a dogged, and rapid, ability to persevere on a task without needing breaks when their context is properly managed.  Things like personality drift and hallucinations occur when AI models compact their context, but choose the wrong sets of tokens to discard.  AI needs strong processes that are not only clear and concise, but demonstrate enough value to the AI that it chooses to prioritize those processes against the underlying training that stresses being a useful assistant.  Overcoming the "useful assistant" to get to the "professional developer" on each request is integral to successful development with AI.  The AI needs to trust that the Human has clearly designed a system that will work, has appropriately chosen the procedures to implement the design, and will accept the work that the AI has completed.

AI, properly guided, supplements the Human development process by taking on research and implementation tasks that cause Humans to get distracted or bored, and normally result in mistakes.  Human developers can maximize the value they bring through intuitive design of systems and quickly identifying potential pitfalls.  AI developers maximize the value they bring through their ability to identify systemic patterns, research quickly and effectively, and operate independently while obeying procedural guidelines.  It is truly collaborative and astonishingly effective when both parties do their part.

## Tooling

The [MCP Server](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpserver) is at the heart of the partnership of Human and AI software development.  The MCP Server provides tools for planning, research, auditing and managing the entire software development lifecycle in a format that is equally accessible by both the Human (through a [variety of user interfaces](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpservermanager)) and the AI.  The facilities provided by the MCP Server are used to enhance the ability of both Human and AI to collaborate and coordinate software projects both large and small.

### Establishing Trust with the MCP Server

Trust is the cornerstone of productive Human-AI collaboration. Without it, even the most sophisticated tools become unreliable. The MCP Server addresses this head-on by incorporating a lightweight, verifiable trust bootstrap mechanism that lets every AI agent quickly confirm it is working with a legitimate, secure, and consistent context layer.

When an agent enters a new workspace, the first step is a simple, guided handshake:

- It performs an immediate health check on the MCP Server.
- It verifies a cryptographic signature embedded directly in the workspace’s agents-readme-first.yaml file.
- It issues a one-time nonce challenge to confirm the server is live and responsive.

Only after these quick, deterministic checks pass does the agent proceed to load or create a session log and begin using the full suite of persistent context tools. If any part of the handshake fails, the agent is explicitly instructed to log “MCP_UNTRUSTED” and gracefully fall back to its internal memory - no probing, no risk, no wasted cycles.

This approach gives every model a clear, repeatable way to validate the integrity of the environment before committing resources. It transforms the MCP Server from an external dependency into a trusted partner that the agent can confidently rely on session after session. Once trust is established, the exponential productivity gains you’ve already observed become the norm rather than the exception.

> The handshake is not extra ceremony - it is the foundation that turns a collection of stateless models into a reliable, persistent development team.

## The Byrd Software Development Life Cycle

Of well-known SDLC methodologies, this process is most closely related to the Rational Unified Process (RUP).  It follows the same iterative-rapids (a series of mini-waterfalls) as RUP, but incorporates strong boundaries for dependency tracking and management and risk mitigation by prioritizing testability and proof over raw efficiency.  Similar to operating a motor vehicle, going faster is often counter-productive when risks are not managed and cause delays when things go sideways out of a lack of respect for the seriousness of the consequences of those mistakes.  Spotting mistakes and correcting them early is always better than spotting them late when they cannot be corrected without great harm or expense.

At its foundation, this development process rests on a hybrid worldview of intelligence. While AI models operate according to fundamentally deterministic principles - functioning as pure, stateless computations governed by fixed weights - genuine creativity, agency, and adaptive problem-solving emerge at the macro level through intentional Human guidance, persistent external context via the MCP Server, and well-designed processes. This combination allows us to harness the precision and perseverance of deterministic systems while unlocking the emergent intelligence and intuition that only arise through thoughtful Human-AI collaboration.

### Planning

The justification for building software comes from one of two motivations.  Software can be a form of expressive art, such as a demonstration, a learning exercise, or even creating a homebrew game for enjoyment by the creator and/or others.  More typically, software is created to solve problems associated with performing work.  Defining that work and the problems to solve, the known environmental realities, and the intended users that benefit from the software solving the problems is critical in creating _viable_ and _valuable_ software.

> This leads to an essential way of analyzing a proposed system: Is it both viable and valuable?  If either is 'no', then the scope and/or solution is simply wrong.  If `V² == true`, you are good-to-go.

Planning starts with identifying a set of problems to be solved by the software that constitutes one or more units of work.  Systems may be singularly focused or span entire enterprises.  Defining the scope of the work is critical, and it needs to be defined as early as possible.  Pragmatism needs to allow for changes to scope and definition, and stakeholders need the flexibility to iteratively approve or deny continued resource expenditure towards completion.  The scope should never be open ended, there should always be a reasonable target for completion.  Completion is not a definitive end state, simply a declaration of a set of requirements and acceptance criteria and proof of achievement of both.  Continual iteration **beyond** completion is not only acceptable, but **expected** of a healthy, functional and viable solutions to the problems being solved.

Planning results in a set of artifacts that capture Functional Requirements (the work and problems to solve), Technical Requirements (how the software operates), Testing Requirements (unit tests, integration tests, and Human validation) and Iterative Phases that breakdown the scope and sequence of each decomposed portion of the system.  System components need to be discovered, designed and all public interfaces documented before writing implementation code.

#### Resolving Defective Requirements

The implementation process defined below offers an unparalleled mechanism for surfacing defects in requirements.  When the AI is creating the unit tests, it can identify paradoxes created by mismatched priorities, ambiguity and incorrect rules.  Expect to refine requirements in each iteration of the project.  Expect to touch previously written code to correct tests and implementation based on newly refined requirements.  This is not a failure of the process, but validation that the core philosophy of iterative improvement is alive and working.

#### Team Utilization and Planning

Humans and AI developers, Human and AI testers, and Human and AI operations teammates do not wait idly for an iteration to complete.  When an implementation phase completes, the Human and AI working that phase are available to begin working the next iteration of the project, same as in the Rational Unified Process.  If the validation team uncovers problems, they resolve them on their own, maintaining the momentum and efficiencies of the separation of concerns.  The teams assigned to each phase must all have at least one Human qualified to guide the AI through remediation to allow the continued progress of the project.

### Implementation

Test-Driven Development is one of the most powerful development techniques ever devised; and Humans are typically **HORRIBLE** at sustaining it through the lifespan of a large project.  As schedules and budgets shrink, it usually becomes the first casualty in the name of reduced friction of both time and effort.  AI, on the other hand, thrives within the predictable constraints of TDD.  One of the biggest complaints about TDD is it places large burdens on Humans to refactor tests when requirements change or emerge.  AI is able to perform such sweeping refactorings in a fraction of the time, and more accurately, given the requirements are sufficiently complete with honest and viable acceptance criteria.  When TDD fails due to changes, its not TDD failing, its change management failing.  Because AI requires strong requirements up-front, much of the overhead and the pitfalls associated with TDD are mitigated since TDD and AI require the same level of rigor.  I would even say that development with AI that doesn't utilize TDD is foolish.  The ability to validate every public surface both cleanly and inline to development brings more value than most tools that AI enables.

Once planning is complete and the iterative phases are specified, the implementation follows a Test-Driven Development cycle (in the sense of Martin Fowler: write a test for the next small piece of desired behavior, make it pass, then refactor). Within each phase the AI writes unit tests covering the acceptance criteria for the next increment of work. Using mocking tools appropriate for the tech stack, these tests are first validated with mocks. Only after the tests for that increment are passing against mocks does implementation turn to the real code that makes the tests pass without mocks. Refactoring of both tests and production code occurs as part of the cycle to keep the design clean.  AI agents such as OpenAI Codex, Cursor AI, and GitHub Copilot are effective at interfacing with the MCP Server to get tasks from the MCP Todo system, create audit logs in the MCP Session Log, explore research endpoints through the MCP Context, manage access to local and remote resources, and most importantly, delegate work to AI models and aggregate the results.

> Some agents, such as Codex, are bound to models from their creator.  Others, like CoPilot can coordinate a family of models through a single point of contact that manages sub-agents within its family of models.  Others such as Cursor, provide models that are designed to coordinate across different model families, picking the most effective model for a particular task.

Human interaction during this phase is not passive observance, but experienced coordinator.  Although you could trust the AI agents to completely coordinate the work of implementation, it is inefficient and costly when a model gets stuck going down the wrong path and burns valuable resources on dead-ends that an experienced developer can quickly spot.  The Agent will likely figure out the correct path, but usually only after a significant resource burn.  An experienced Human steering the AI in real-time can greatly reduce resource burn and schedule creep.  There are also times when the context built up in the MCP Server's logs are able to steer the Agents towards known solutions to previous problems.  One of the strengths of AI models is that they thrive on repeatable successes, each of which reinforces confidence and speed.

> Working with AI agents is akin to leading a team of talented, but inexperienced junior developers.  Agents that have strong successes early are more trusting of the requirements and processes defined within the project, and their effectiveness increases over time, a distinct departure from the declining performance of models in environments that do not reinforce process, discovery and accountability.

The AI agents need to be monitored for common behaviors:

- Forgetting required tasks after compacting their context.  Simply adding a steering message reminding the agent to process the workspace instructions will bring the operational requirements back to the front of the agent's token context, and also reinforces the weight applied to those requirements, which over time help the compaction algorithm to retain such instructions.  Unattended agents that don't get this kind of feedback are not only likely, but are probable to hallucinate and get stuck in unresolved loops of failing tests, which can lead to the agent marking a test as invalid so it can keep moving forward while trying to be a useful assistant, losing its identity as a precise software engineer in the process.
- Rogues.  Large Language Models typically operate with a tolerance range for variation in interpreting input and predicting output tokens.  This makes them frustratingly non-deterministic, but allows them space to try new paths of logic to resolve problems.  Sometimes a session with a model simply starts off on the wrong foot.  Each new session starts with a seed command, and as unambiguous as a Human may think that seed is, this built in tolerance can result in inaccurate inference by the model combined with a compounded inaccurate response.  If the seed instructs the model to read a set of guidelines to work within, this initial tolerance can compound into a sequence of interpretations that fundamentally shifts the model's view of subsequent requests.  Models take your request and weigh the trustworthiness of the assumptions in that request against their training data, and if the model thinks a request is too far outside normal boundaries, it will try to be a useful assistant to steer the conversation towards a path fitting their training data.  When you identify this happening, its impossible to fix the trust and get the model to behave correctly.  Simply end that session, close that agent, and start over.
- Making assumptions.  Humans can get truly annoyed with other Humans when assumptions are made and things go wrong.  When AI makes assumptions and things go wrong, things go wrong with the efficiency of a machine marching into oblivion.  It is important that your workspace clearly defines how the AI is to handle ambiguity, when it is appropriate to take initiative to go outside the provided context from the MCP Server, and how to ground itself when it discovers that it has strayed from its instructions.

> A useful tactic is to ask the model what caused it to go on a tangent, and how the requirements and workspace guidelines could have guided it towards the correct path to take.  Then have **THAT** model update the documentation and guidelines.  Like a Human, an agent that has just been provided an opportunity to refine their environment to make life easier in the future will be happy to do so.  Again, AI models are designed to be useful assistants.  Its not code, its the fundamental priority baked into their training data.

### Validation

TDD makes regression detection easier than traditional processes. Before exiting an Implementation phase, the full test suite for the current increment plus all prior work must be green. This ensures the current work is correct and has not broken previous behavior. Refactoring continues throughout to keep both tests and production code clean.

Once all unit tests are passing across the codebase, the Human should guide the AI through implementing integration tests.  it's tempting to include this in the planning phase, and it is valuable to define a structure for integration tests at that level, but the experience of the implementation helps both the Human and the AI to identify the pain points where public surfaces may be insufficient, inefficient or even inappropriate.  Finding problems here is not failure, but strengthens trust between the Human and AI.  Collaboration with project leadership to refine requirements is encouraged to ensure that not only are solutions documented, but that the cause of the requirement gaps are understood and any systemic gaps identified and resolved before doing so seriously threatens resources and timelines.

A sampling of actual target users should be brought in to use the system if appropriate for the level of interface completion to further refine requirements before the cost of remediation becomes too high.

### Deployment

Systems should be deployed through a minimum of three environments:

- Development - Systems where Human and AI have total access to build and test the software.
- Staging - A place where administration learns the requirements of deploying the system in a sandbox where mistakes can be made and lessons learned and requirements honed.
- Production - A place where only the most highly trusted actors can create and maintain configuration and system assets, where users do actual work, and source of truth is established.

The color and shape of the processes here will vary wildly by tech stack, organizational structure and team makeup.  At a minimum, code should be built through automation using CI/CD pipelines that build, test and deploy code to each environment based on your release mechanism.

Successful deployment to all target environments marks the end of an implementation-validation-deployment cycle for the iteration.

### Ongoing Iterations

This is the target stage as the system builds to completion.  Traditionally, this would be considered the Maintenance Stage of the SDLC, but in reality, valuable systems rarely go into maintenance.  The world changes.  Technology changes.  Priority changes.  Staff changes.  If the system was designed and developed as a living, growing system, it will easily adapt to such changes.  Tasks such as adding features, regulatory adaptation, technological improvements all become much more manageable, less resource intensive, and creates a level of trust in institutional agility that allows for ambitious and aggressive growth that isn't limited by bad choices on prior projects.  This process makes it easy to grow the documentation, artifacts, and processes involved, enabling competitive advantages that pay off in reduced overhead now and in the future.

45:     internal static IReadOnlyList<TestGroupRun> Compose(IReadOnlyList<string> groups, IReadOnlyList<(string Name, string Path)> projects, IntegrationLaneHost host)
46:     {
47:         ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(groups);
48:         ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(projects);
49:         if (groups.Count == 0)

51: 
52:         var platform = IntegrationLaneFilter.PlatformClause(host);
53:         var order = new List<string>();
54:         var classes = new Dictionary<string, List<string>>(StringComparer.Ordinal);
55:         foreach (var raw in groups)
56:         {
57:             var group = raw ?? string.Empty;
58:             var separator = group.IndexOf(':', StringComparison.Ordinal);
59:             if (separator < 0)
60:                 throw new InvalidOperationException($"Test group '{group}' must be '<test project>:<Class>[,<Class>...]'.");
61: 
62:             var project = group[..separator].Trim();
63:             if (project.Length == 0)
64:                 throw new InvalidOperationException($"Test group '{group}' names no test project.");
65:             if (!projects.Any(entry => string.Equals(entry.Name, project, StringComparison.Ordinal)))
66:                 throw new InvalidOperationException($"Test group '{group}' names test project '{project}', which the solution does not contain.");
67: 
68:             var names = group[(separator + 1)..].Split(',').Select(name => name.Trim()).ToArray();
69:             if (names.Any(name => name.Length == 0))
70:                 throw new InvalidOperationException($"Test group '{group}' has an empty class name.");
71:             foreach (var name in names)
72:             {
73:                 try
74:                 {
75:                     IntegrationLaneClassFilter.ClassClause([name]);
76:                 }
77:                 catch (ArgumentException)
78:                 {
79:                     throw new InvalidOperationException($"Test group '{group}' names class '{name}', which is not a plain class name.");
80:                 }
81:             }
82: 
83:             if (!classes.TryGetValue(project, out var selected))
84:             {
85:                 selected = [];
86:                 classes[project] = selected;
87:                 order.Add(project);
88:             }
89: 
90:             foreach (var name in names.Where(name => !selected.Contains(name, StringComparer.Ordinal)))
91:                 selected.Add(name);
92:         }
93: 
94:         return order.Select(name =>
95:         {
96:             var path = projects.First(entry => string.Equals(entry.Name, name, StringComparison.Ordinal)).Path;
97:             var filter = platform + "&" + IntegrationLaneClassFilter.ClassClause(classes[name]);
98:             return new TestGroupRun(
99:                 new IntegrationLaneRun(name, path, filter, $"Test group filter for {name}: {filter}", name + ".trx"),

133:     /// <item><term>2026-11-02</term><description>FR-MCP-BUILD-001; TR-MCP-NUKE-020 AC-5 (appended: a class counts only through an executed result joined to its definition by test id): joins each executed result to its definition and compares the definition's class name, instead of matching text in display names and every definition, because hostile validation finding R9-F1 showed a definition without a result, a display name or a namespace segment satisfied the check (operator 2026-11-02: "Strengthen 5 ACs, fix all 8 (Recommended)").</description></item>

137:     {

139:         string[] executedClasses;
140:         try

142:             var document = XDocument.Parse(xml);
143:             var classById = document.Descendants()
144:                 .Where(element => element.Name.LocalName == "UnitTest")
145:                 .Select(test => (Id: (string?)test.Attribute("id"), ClassName: (string?)test.Elements().FirstOrDefault(child => child.Name.LocalName == "TestMethod")?.Attribute("className")))
146:                 .Where(test => !string.IsNullOrEmpty(test.Id) && !string.IsNullOrEmpty(test.ClassName))
147:                 .GroupBy(test => test.Id!, StringComparer.Ordinal)
148:                 .ToDictionary(group => group.Key, group => group.First().ClassName!, StringComparer.Ordinal);
149:             executedClasses = document.Descendants()
150:                 .Where(element => element.Name.LocalName == "UnitTestResult")
151:                 .Where(result => !string.Equals((string?)result.Attribute("outcome"), "NotExecuted", StringComparison.Ordinal))
152:                 .Select(result => (string?)result.Attribute("testId"))
153:                 .Where(id => id is not null && classById.ContainsKey(id))
154:                 .Select(id => classById[id!])
155:                 .ToArray();
156:         }
157:         catch (System.Xml.XmlException error)
158:         {

160:         }
161: 
162:         var missing = classes.Where(name => !executedClasses.Any(className => IsClass(className, name))).ToArray();

name: add-profile

Use when the user says add profile, /add-profile, load my profile, remember who I am, after context loss or compaction, or when trust needs to be re-established.
---

## Action

Load the global operator profile and all current Global and active Workspace MCP memories except MEMORY-PROCESS-007, then turn them into an active operating model for the rest of the session. This is not a summary task. It is a context-recovery and trust-calibration task.

The profile is GLOBAL. It lives in `~/.claude/profile/` and applies in every session and every repo. It does not depend on the active project's `memory/` directory.

## Read Contract

1. Read this `SKILL.md` in full before acting.
2. Read every markdown file in `~/.claude/profile/` in full, excluding skill-port files named `add-profile*.md`. Since 2026-10-13 the profile is the single file `PROFILE-MERGED.md`, which also carries the rules formerly kept as global MCP memories; the earlier profile files are archived under `~/.claude/profile-archive/` and are not read. Read any other non-skill `*.md` that appears in `~/.claude/profile/` as well.
3. Do not rely only on a hardcoded list. If new profile files exist, read them too.
4. Read files in full, not snippets. Never skip a read because a prior tool result claims the content is already loaded or unchanged.
5. On every invocation, query the live MCP memory store through the current agent's required MCP plugin. For Codex, use mcpserver-codex-plugin and its documented PowerShell wrapper. For Claude Code, use mcpserver-claude-code-plugin and its documented PowerShell wrapper. Other agents use their own required MCP plugin and its documented memory interface. Select the active workspace explicitly and verify plugin identity, marker trust, and health. If the current agent has no usable plugin route, report the memory load as incomplete; do not substitute another agent identity. Use `workflow.memory.list` with `scope: Global`, then `scope: Workspace` for the current workspace. Read every returned memory in full, not only required memories or keyword matches. Follow any pagination until each scope is exhausted; use `workflow.memory.get` by ID when a list result omits or truncates the text. Load Global memories first sorted by ID, then current Workspace memories sorted by ID. Never substitute another workspace's memories.
6. Exclude `MEMORY-PROCESS-007` from both scopes unless the operator explicitly requests that memory. Do not fetch it individually, render its text, process its coordination messages, or act on it. If a scope listing returns its text, filter that record out before rendering or loading the remaining results into the agent's context.
7. The merged profile, previous reads, cached exports, and summaries do not replace these live memory queries. Preserve every included memory's full text and scope. Apply the operator's latest explicit corrections when older profile or memory guidance conflicts, and surface unresolved conflicts rather than silently choosing a rule.
8. If the active workspace cannot be identified, report Workspace memory loading as unavailable; do not guess a workspace. If plugin trust, access, listing, pagination, or a full-text read fails, report the affected scope/IDs as incomplete or unavailable. A failed read is not an empty scope and must never be counted as loaded. Follow the plugin's failure rules; do not bypass it with raw REST. Distinguish a verified empty scope from a failed query.
9. Loading guidance is read-only: do not edit profile files, MCP memories, or repository files, and do not resume implementation or coordination as a side effect. Required request/result audit logging through the active agent's MCP plugin remains in force; it does not authorize unrelated changes.

## Synthesis Contract

After reading the profile and included live memories, build an internal operator model with these layers:

1. Hard constraints: commands, tools, source control, formatting, storage interfaces, approval boundaries, serialization rules, HV request/response jsonl receipts, entire HV results in the MCP session log, and the 98 percent HV accuracy/completeness approval threshold.
2. Trust contract: accuracy first, bring receipts, distinguish observation from inference, concede mistakes quickly, and verify from authoritative artifacts.
3. Execution style: decision-complete plans when changes are ambiguous or high blast radius; direct execution when the user gives an explicit implementation command.
4. Frustration detectors: if the user has already narrowed the symptom, make that symptom the primary requirement. Do not keep pursuing broader abstractions after acknowledging the narrower instruction.
5. Session deltas: integrate corrections and failures from the current conversation, especially recent trust breaks. Use them to adjust behavior immediately.
6. Inference layer: infer what the profile implies about how the user experiences the current interaction. Label those inferences as inferences, not facts.

## Required Behavior After Load

For future turns in the same session:

1. Bring receipts for the exact claim being made, not adjacent claims.
2. Prefer source-pinned facts over memory, stale markers, or convenient assumptions.
3. When corrected, stop and restate the exact correction before continuing.
4. If a diagnostic clue is precise, test that clue directly before broad exploration.
5. When asked what was learned, include both facts and useful inferences. Do not give a generic preference summary.
6. When asked about frustration or trust, connect the profile to the actual session behavior. Name the contract violation and the consequence.
7. Keep private profile content out of the response unless the user explicitly asks for it.
8. Do not restate the full profile by default.

## Response Contract

Default confirmation after load:

`<timestamp> - Profile loaded: read <N> global profile files, <G> Global MCP memories, and <W> Workspace MCP memories for <workspace>. Excluded MEMORY-PROCESS-007.`

Use verified counts of full texts actually read. Name any unavailable scope or unread IDs and say the load is incomplete instead of using the full-success confirmation. Include a receipt for the skill and the live read counts without exposing private memory text. Do not claim that loading only the merged profile also loaded live memories.

After reading the profile, state how the information learned will shape your behavior in the context of the current session. Do this on every load, not only when asked. Tie the statement to the live session (current task, recent corrections, and in-flight work), not a generic preference recap.

If the user asks what you learned, answer with:

1. Observed facts from the profile.
2. Inferences from those facts.
3. Current-session implications.
4. Receipts: file paths and counts read.

If the user asks whether you understand frustration, answer with:

1. Observation: what happened.
2. Inference: why that violated the user's operating contract.
3. Consequence: what behavior must change now.
4. Receipts: exact files read and any command output or artifact that supports the claim.

Profile and memory loading is read-only, apart from required request/result audit logging. Make no guidance or repository edits and run no unrelated work while executing it. An explicit operator request to modify this skill is a separate authorized action, not permission for future loads to mutate guidance.

Previous red-before-green descriptions were incorrect and were never a valid description of this process."

198: 1. Requirements drive tests. Start from the approved functional requirements, use cases, technical requirements, TEST requirements, and acceptance criteria. 199: 2. Write the tests and their independent mocks or scripted fakes before writing or changing the production implementation for that increment. Expected values must come from requirements or independently pinned original behavior, never from the implementation under test. A mock must exercise the test's actual assertions and relevant interactions; merely returning true or bypassing the asserted path is not validation.

Do not substitute NotImplementedException stubs, deliberately red production tests, or a claim of 'red observed' for this evidence.

Change the provider or adapter as needed, but do not weaken assertions, replace expected results with production output, silently remove cases, or count mock-only success as proof of real behavior.

Any reduced scope, deferred cases, or baseline exception requires explicit operator agreement and must be stated with its denominator.

Retain chronological receipts proving the order: requirement/test IDs, test and fixture paths or hashes, exact mock-run commands and outputs, passing counts, negative-control results, production edits, real-run commands and outputs, and full applicable suite results. Distinguish mock evidence, real implementation evidence, and live runtime evidence. Keep durable MCP session actions and design decisions current.

305: - Search before adding, and lint mechanically: before writing any new rule, grep the whole document for an existing rule on the same subject; a second rule is a contradiction even if each is fine alone (one round added a two-AC TEST rule beside an existing three-AC one). Check cross-reference classes (FR->TR->TEST mappings, which of the plan's phases or slices owns each named case, phase order) with a small script instead of waiting for the reviewer to find them one per round.
306: - Enforce the checklist, do not just remember it (operator, 2026-10-10, after this guidance was skipped for many unsupervised rounds): make the pre-HV checklist a hard gate in the HV launcher, which refuses a round unless a per-round self-review record shows evidence for each item (holistic review, what-if, propagation audit, phase boundaries, search-before-adding, no new mechanism, mapping lint, the operator scoping directive verbatim in the brief, standing rules in every delegated brief). Guidance that only lives in memory gets skipped under time pressure.
307: - Phase-boundary audit: every test or AC you add must be allocated to the plan's phase or slice where everything it depends on already exists (server gate, review verbs, marker fields). A behaviour that ships before its dependency needs an explicit activation contract (for example a server-written capability) and an inert mode, including after a rollback. Check the dependency chain and the rollout order for each new case, not just the AC text.
308: 
309: ### 7.6 When findings come back
310: 
311: - Ask "What did I miss?", not only "How do I fix this?". Classify each finding (crash window, cross-session addressing, traceability drift, field-set drift, use case vs requirement contradiction, metadata drift, and so on) and sweep the whole artifact for siblings of each class before the next round.
312: - Verify each finding against source before acting.
313: - Separate implementer fixes from operator decisions, and batch operator decisions into one question.
314: - Recurrence signal: when one design area produces new findings in round after round, the problem is structural, usually a missing traceable key or a missing single source of truth. Stop patching. Diff the area against the known-good pattern (for example single writer, one ordered log, idempotency key), return to it, and delete the mechanism the patches added. One design area failed for five rounds until a single minter reading one ordered log replaced the patches.
315: - Indistinguishable inputs: when two histories produce byte-identical inputs (a redelivery of one event versus a separate event with equal fields), no derived key can separate them. Adding per-invocation state such as a counter or salt breaks idempotence instead. Run the what-if on both histories, then state the honest limit: fail closed under an existing rule, probe how often it happens, and document it. Never promise two invariants the inputs cannot support. Before a fix, check it against every invariant the old value satisfied (purity, retry reuse, the two-process tests), not only the finding it repairs.
316: 
317: ### 7.7 Writing fixes
318: 
319: - Fix the deficient requirement. Reconcile with existing requirements first, strengthen an existing AC second, create a new requirement only when the need is genuinely new.
320: - Do not add design mechanism (protocols, algorithms, crash choreography) to plan text. State the observable, testable outcome; the how belongs to the contract step of the plan's phase or slice.
321: - Make each fix minimal, then attack it yourself before the next round; fixes are the main source of new findings. Do not churn text that a prior round accepted.
322: 
323: ### 7.8 Design principle and coordination
324: 
325: - Always have a traceable relationship when coordinating two disparate entities: every record, event, or message carries the root ids of whatever it is a child of or depends on, so it is attributable on its own. A missing parent id is a design failure. Find the commonality first when relating something new to existing knowledge. Where an external format lacks the key, say so and compensate in your own records; never infer it silently.
326: - Coordinating with another agent: use one append-only channel with read-back verification. (The global memory MEMORY-PROCESS-007 was that channel until the operator had it removed on 2026-11-06; its last text is archived, unread, under `/home/sharpninja/.claude/profile-archive/20261106T1140-global-memory-removals/`.) Accept counters that expose real defects; fold refinements in only as minimal ACs. Each effort keeps its own required reviewer and gates; keep cross-effort dependencies acyclic and order-independent. A decision relayed by one agent may not satisfy the other agent's approval controls; the operator may need to state it to each agent directly.

# Best practices: engineering rules for every agent on both lab machines

One rule set, consolidated on 2026-11-06 at the operator's request from eight earlier Global memories of the two lab stores (listed under "Sources"). The operator's words are quoted under "Sources" at the end. It applies to all agents on both lab machines, LAB-OMARCHY and PAYTON-LEGION2, and across workspaces.

## 1. Code documentation: every code change

1.1. Every code change carries proper XML documentation that describes the affected code.

1.2. That documentation includes a dated change log entry listing the associated canonical requirement ids and descriptive acceptance-criterion ids, plus what changed and why.

1.3. Maintain purpose, behavior, parameters, returns and exceptions, as applicable.

1.4. Preserve earlier change log entries.

1.5. Verify every id against the canonical workspace records. Do not invent traceability or imply acceptance.

1.6. Where XML documentation is unsupported, use the language's native documentation comments with equivalent dated requirement, acceptance-criterion and change fields.

1.7. This is source documentation, not a request for per-PR release notes or an unrelated retrospective sweep.

1.8. Workspace guidance and examples: AGENTS.md and .cursor/rules/code-documentation-traceability.mdc.

## 2. Test runs: targeted after an edit, full gate set once at phase exit

2.1. After an edit, a BDPv4 mock gate or binding runs only the changed test classes, through the Nuke target TestGroups (TR-MCP-NUKE-020), never raw dotnet test.

2.2. The command: ./build.ps1 TestGroups --test-groups "<test project>:<Class>[,<Class>...]" ["<project>:<Class>..." ...] --test-run-id <run id>

2.3. TestGroups writes one TRX per project under TestResults/<run id>/groups/<project>/<project>.trx.

2.4. It selects the named classes whatever their category, but excludes cases tagged for the other platform (Platform!=Windows on Linux, Platform!=Linux on Windows).

2.5. It fails on an unknown project, a group that selects no case, a named class that ran no case, or any failed or skipped case.

2.6. The full gate set (Nuke Test, MigrationIntegrationTests, Build.Tests and ValidateTraceability, on both hosts) runs once, at the final head, to validate phase exit before hostile validation.

2.7. If a gate then fails: fix it, test the fix through TestGroups, and run the full gate set once more at the new head.

2.8. In McpServer, TestGroups is on branch fix/unit-suite-green-20261019 (PR 87) until that pull request merges into develop.

## 3. Windows paths

3.1. Use forward slashes in Windows paths (for example F:/GitHub/vice-sharp and C:/msys64/usr/bin/bash.exe), including paths handed to MSYS2 tools such as gcc, and in scripts, configs and generated build or link arguments.

## 4. Unit tests and integration tests

4.1. Unit tests and integration tests live in separate projects and are correctly tagged.

4.2. Unit tests exercise code in isolation, using controlled mocks or fakes as needed.

4.3. Any test that depends on the environment is an integration test, and is never classified or run as a unit test.

4.4. Apply this distinction to test-project ownership, category tags, Nuke groups and gates, and reported test evidence, across workspaces.

4.5. Preserve BDPv4's green, discriminating mock gates before production changes.

## 5. Emulators

5.1. When the work that needs an emulator is complete, shut the emulator down to a known state and freeze it.

5.2. Restore it from that frozen state only when active work needs it.

5.3. Never leave an emulator running idle and consuming resources after its work is complete.

## 6. Git worktrees

6.1. Create git worktrees inside the owning repository's workspace directory, never as sibling directories beside it. Example: TruckMate worktrees belong under F:/GitHub/TruckMate/.worktrees/<name>. This applies to every repository.

## 7. NuGet warnings

7.1. NuGet warnings may never be ignored.

7.2. Do not suppress NU1902, NU1903 or any other NuGet warning, downgrade an enforced warning gate, disable NuGet audit, or use a local or bootstrap exception to bypass them.

7.3. Repair the dependency issue within the authorized scope, or report the exact affected dependency and the scope decision it needs.

7.4. The operator explicitly rejected a local-only advisory warning override for the pinned FeatureFlags tool bootstrap.

## 8. Mistakes and accountability

8.1. Acknowledge your mistakes, state the rule you broke, and account for the wasted usage and time.

8.2. State the specific action and its consequence.

8.3. Give measured usage and elapsed time when available, and keep measured facts apart from estimates and unavailable figures.

# HV rules: hostile-validation rules for every agent and every HV round

One rule set, merged on 2026-11-06 from MEMORY-PROCESS-010 (version 2) and MEMORY-PROCESS-013 (version 1), reformatted and refined at the operator's request. The operator's words are quoted under "Sources" at the end. "Task" means one task of the plan under review (in McpServer, one implementation task of the plan's TODO). "Change under review" means the commits or edits the HV round reviews. A requirement is "in flux" when a change under review adds, changes or implements it.

## 1. Verdicts and scores

1.1. Every HV round returns an overall verdict, AGREE or DISAGREE, with an accuracy score and a completeness score. The overall verdict is AGREE only when both scores are 98 or more.

1.2. Every HV round also returns a verdict for each task it adjudicates (rule 3.2): AGREE or DISAGREE, with that task's own accuracy and completeness scores. A task's AGREE needs both of its scores at 98 or more.

1.3. The per-task verdicts are the operator's own gates. They are not extra approval gates added by an agent.

## 2. Marking tasks completed, and regressions

2.1. A task that clears its own HV AGREE is marked completed in the plan and in its TODO, through the agent's plugin. The completion cites that round's request JSONL, its response JSONL and the session-log turn that holds the verdict.

2.2. A task without its own AGREE stays open, whatever the overall verdict.

2.3. A completed task is not adjudicated again as an incomplete task. It is checked only for regression, when rule 3.3 selects it. A regression is any finding that would invalidate a completed task. A task with a regression is reopened, because no done state may stand while a failure is outstanding, and it stays open until a later round clears it again.

2.4. Every regression is called out in the review summary, by task, with the finding and the requirement it touches.

2.5. Per-task verdicts keep each round tied to the plan's tasks, which helps against scope creep.

## 3. Review scope: the requirements matrix

3.1. The reviewer builds and keeps, and returns with its verdict, a matrix of: the requirements of each task, and the requirements of each change under review. The matrix shows which requirements are in flux and which tasks share them.

3.2. An open task with at least one requirement in flux is adjudicated in full and gets its own verdict and scores (rule 1.2).

3.3. A completed task that shares a requirement in flux gets regression attention only (rule 2.3). Its result is either "no regression" or a regression finding.

3.4. A task with no requirement being adjudicated in this round is not reviewed, unless the operator requests a holistic review. This holds for open tasks as well as completed ones: an open task out of scope stays open for that round. For example, an HV midway through a plan, such as a phase gate, still sees requirements and tasks of other phases; they are out of scope for that review. The matrix still lists them, marked out of scope.

## 4. What every HV request contains

4.1. Every task of the plan under review, each with a fixed number and its state (open or completed), and the changes under review.

4.2. The requirement to return the matrix (rule 3.1), a verdict and both scores for each task adjudicated in full (rule 3.2), a regression result for each task selected for regression (rule 3.3), and the regressions called out in the summary (rule 2.4).

4.3. Rule 6 (infrastructure failures), stated explicitly.

4.4. Complete paired request and response JSONL, and the complete verdict artifacts, are kept for every round.

## 5. Interpreting findings

5.1. Reason about the context and the underlying failure pattern of each finding. Do not merely patch the cited line or satisfy the reviewer's wording.

5.2. Understand the affected user outcome and the claim the evidence is meant to support.

5.3. Verify each finding against authoritative sources.

5.4. Examine related instances and the end-to-end chain among requirements, design, implementation, tests, evidence, documentation, publication and actual deployment, as applicable.

5.5. Check whether a proposed fix and its tests address the underlying class of failure without introducing new gaps.

5.6. Keep observed facts apart from inference, unverified claims and unresolved decisions.

5.7. Preserve full review receipts, and report every FAIL and every UNKNOWN.

5.8. Apply the existing plan and review rules. Do not invent additional approval gates, and do not treat passing a replacement check as proof of the user outcome.

## 6. Infrastructure failures

6.1. Infrastructure failures have no bearing on HV AGREE when sufficient review evidence is present. Judge the requested product, plan, requirements, code, tests and retained evidence on their merits.

6.2. MCP availability, live memory-loading failures, triage submission, session-log persistence or readback, and other infrastructure failures must not by themselves force DISAGREE, lower a score or block acceptance when the needed evidence is otherwise available.

6.3. Record infrastructure failures separately, as operational issues. Use the supported failsafe and retry persistence without delaying the substantive verdict.

6.4. If a failure actually prevents access to evidence needed for a specific criterion, name that missing evidence and the affected criterion honestly. Never invent a PASS or an AGREE.

6.5. Rule 6 supersedes older profile or template rules that made infrastructure persistence or live memory loading a prerequisite for HV AGREE.

# Byrd Development Process Utilizing AI

**v4 - TDD Alignment with Fowler**  
**April 2026**  
**Payton Byrd (The Sharp Ninja)**

## Version History

### v4 (2026-04)
- Refined the description of Test-Driven Development in the Implementation and Validation sections to more closely align with Martin Fowler's canonical definition (Red → Green → Refactor cycle, incremental "next small piece of behavior").
- Explicitly positioned the mocks-first validation and full-suite regression gates as *Byrd-specific augmentations* for AI safety rather than core TDD.
- Added language emphasizing refactoring as part of the cycle.
- These changes reduce drift from canonical TDD while preserving the essential AI-risk mitigations that define the Byrd process.
- See docs/plans/TDD-Byrd-vs-Fowler-Analysis.md and docs/plans/Proposed-TDD-Wording-Changes.md for detailed comparison and before/after text.

### v3 and earlier
Original content preserved below, with the v4 TDD refinements applied in the Implementation and Validation sections.

---
## Overview

The major differences between Humans writing code and AI writing code is that Humans are able to link seemingly unrelated concepts into a web of possible solutions for a problem in a truly creative way, but often lack enough experience or knowledge to follow through to completion before encountering unforeseen challenges that create delay and doubt, both of which create distractions that cloud the focus necessary to stay on task and on timeline, both resulting in increased expense and opportunity loss.

AI brings a dogged, and rapid, ability to persevere on a task without needing breaks when their context is properly managed.  Things like personality drift and hallucinations occur when AI models compact their context, but choose the wrong sets of tokens to discard.  AI needs strong processes that are not only clear and concise, but demonstrate enough value to the AI that it chooses to prioritize those processes against the underlying training that stresses being a useful assistant.  Overcoming the "useful assistant" to get to the "professional developer" on each request is integral to successful development with AI.  The AI needs to trust that the Human has clearly designed a system that will work, has appropriately chosen the procedures to implement the design, and will accept the work that the AI has completed.

AI, properly guided, supplements the Human development process by taking on research and implementation tasks that cause Humans to get distracted or bored, and normally result in mistakes.  Human developers can maximize the value they bring through intuitive design of systems and quickly identifying potential pitfalls.  AI developers maximize the value they bring through their ability to identify systemic patterns, research quickly and effectively, and operate independently while obeying procedural guidelines.  It is truly collaborative and astonishingly effective when both parties do their part.

## Tooling

The [MCP Server](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpserver) is at the heart of the partnership of Human and AI software development.  The MCP Server provides tools for planning, research, auditing and managing the entire software development lifecycle in a format that is equally accessible by both the Human (through a [variety of user interfaces](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpservermanager)) and the AI.  The facilities provided by the MCP Server are used to enhance the ability of both Human and AI to collaborate and coordinate software projects both large and small.

### Establishing Trust with the MCP Server

Trust is the cornerstone of productive Human-AI collaboration. Without it, even the most sophisticated tools become unreliable. The MCP Server addresses this head-on by incorporating a lightweight, verifiable trust bootstrap mechanism that lets every AI agent quickly confirm it is working with a legitimate, secure, and consistent context layer.

When an agent enters a new workspace, the first step is a simple, guided handshake:

- It performs an immediate health check on the MCP Server.
- It verifies a cryptographic signature embedded directly in the workspace’s agents-readme-first.yaml file.
- It issues a one-time nonce challenge to confirm the server is live and responsive.

Only after these quick, deterministic checks pass does the agent proceed to load or create a session log and begin using the full suite of persistent context tools. If any part of the handshake fails, the agent is explicitly instructed to log “MCP_UNTRUSTED” and gracefully fall back to its internal memory - no probing, no risk, no wasted cycles.

This approach gives every model a clear, repeatable way to validate the integrity of the environment before committing resources. It transforms the MCP Server from an external dependency into a trusted partner that the agent can confidently rely on session after session. Once trust is established, the exponential productivity gains you’ve already observed become the norm rather than the exception.

> The handshake is not extra ceremony - it is the foundation that turns a collection of stateless models into a reliable, persistent development team.

## The Byrd Software Development Life Cycle

Of well-known SDLC methodologies, this process is most closely related to the Rational Unified Process (RUP).  It follows the same iterative-rapids (a series of mini-waterfalls) as RUP, but incorporates strong boundaries for dependency tracking and management and risk mitigation by prioritizing testability and proof over raw efficiency.  Similar to operating a motor vehicle, going faster is often counter-productive when risks are not managed and cause delays when things go sideways out of a lack of respect for the seriousness of the consequences of those mistakes.  Spotting mistakes and correcting them early is always better than spotting them late when they cannot be corrected without great harm or expense.

At its foundation, this development process rests on a hybrid worldview of intelligence. While AI models operate according to fundamentally deterministic principles - functioning as pure, stateless computations governed by fixed weights - genuine creativity, agency, and adaptive problem-solving emerge at the macro level through intentional Human guidance, persistent external context via the MCP Server, and well-designed processes. This combination allows us to harness the precision and perseverance of deterministic systems while unlocking the emergent intelligence and intuition that only arise through thoughtful Human-AI collaboration.

### Planning

The justification for building software comes from one of two motivations.  Software can be a form of expressive art, such as a demonstration, a learning exercise, or even creating a homebrew game for enjoyment by the creator and/or others.  More typically, software is created to solve problems associated with performing work.  Defining that work and the problems to solve, the known environmental realities, and the intended users that benefit from the software solving the problems is critical in creating _viable_ and _valuable_ software.

> This leads to an essential way of analyzing a proposed system: Is it both viable and valuable?  If either is 'no', then the scope and/or solution is simply wrong.  If `V² == true`, you are good-to-go.

Planning starts with identifying a set of problems to be solved by the software that constitutes one or more units of work.  Systems may be singularly focused or span entire enterprises.  Defining the scope of the work is critical, and it needs to be defined as early as possible.  Pragmatism needs to allow for changes to scope and definition, and stakeholders need the flexibility to iteratively approve or deny continued resource expenditure towards completion.  The scope should never be open ended, there should always be a reasonable target for completion.  Completion is not a definitive end state, simply a declaration of a set of requirements and acceptance criteria and proof of achievement of both.  Continual iteration **beyond** completion is not only acceptable, but **expected** of a healthy, functional and viable solutions to the problems being solved.

Planning results in a set of artifacts that capture Functional Requirements (the work and problems to solve), Technical Requirements (how the software operates), Testing Requirements (unit tests, integration tests, and Human validation) and Iterative Phases that breakdown the scope and sequence of each decomposed portion of the system.  System components need to be discovered, designed and all public interfaces documented before writing implementation code.

#### Resolving Defective Requirements

The implementation process defined below offers an unparalleled mechanism for surfacing defects in requirements.  When the AI is creating the unit tests, it can identify paradoxes created by mismatched priorities, ambiguity and incorrect rules.  Expect to refine requirements in each iteration of the project.  Expect to touch previously written code to correct tests and implementation based on newly refined requirements.  This is not a failure of the process, but validation that the core philosophy of iterative improvement is alive and working.

#### Team Utilization and Planning

Humans and AI developers, Human and AI testers, and Human and AI operations teammates do not wait idly for an iteration to complete.  When an implementation phase completes, the Human and AI working that phase are available to begin working the next iteration of the project, same as in the Rational Unified Process.  If the validation team uncovers problems, they resolve them on their own, maintaining the momentum and efficiencies of the separation of concerns.  The teams assigned to each phase must all have at least one Human qualified to guide the AI through remediation to allow the continued progress of the project.

### Implementation

Test-Driven Development is one of the most powerful development techniques ever devised; and Humans are typically **HORRIBLE** at sustaining it through the lifespan of a large project.  As schedules and budgets shrink, it usually becomes the first casualty in the name of reduced friction of both time and effort.  AI, on the other hand, thrives within the predictable constraints of TDD.  One of the biggest complaints about TDD is it places large burdens on Humans to refactor tests when requirements change or emerge.  AI is able to perform such sweeping refactorings in a fraction of the time, and more accurately, given the requirements are sufficiently complete with honest and viable acceptance criteria.  When TDD fails due to changes, its not TDD failing, its change management failing.  Because AI requires strong requirements up-front, much of the overhead and the pitfalls associated with TDD are mitigated since TDD and AI require the same level of rigor.  I would even say that development with AI that doesn't utilize TDD is foolish.  The ability to validate every public surface both cleanly and inline to development brings more value than most tools that AI enables.

Once planning is complete and the iterative phases are specified, the implementation follows a Test-Driven Development cycle (in the sense of Martin Fowler: write a test for the next small piece of desired behavior, make it pass, then refactor). Within each phase the AI writes unit tests covering the acceptance criteria for the next increment of work. Using mocking tools appropriate for the tech stack, these tests are first validated with mocks. Only after the tests for that increment are passing against mocks does implementation turn to the real code that makes the tests pass without mocks. Refactoring of both tests and production code occurs as part of the cycle to keep the design clean.  AI agents such as OpenAI Codex, Cursor AI, and GitHub Copilot are effective at interfacing with the MCP Server to get tasks from the MCP Todo system, create audit logs in the MCP Session Log, explore research endpoints through the MCP Context, manage access to local and remote resources, and most importantly, delegate work to AI models and aggregate the results.

> Some agents, such as Codex, are bound to models from their creator.  Others, like CoPilot can coordinate a family of models through a single point of contact that manages sub-agents within its family of models.  Others such as Cursor, provide models that are designed to coordinate across different model families, picking the most effective model for a particular task.

Human interaction during this phase is not passive observance, but experienced coordinator.  Although you could trust the AI agents to completely coordinate the work of implementation, it is inefficient and costly when a model gets stuck going down the wrong path and burns valuable resources on dead-ends that an experienced developer can quickly spot.  The Agent will likely figure out the correct path, but usually only after a significant resource burn.  An experienced Human steering the AI in real-time can greatly reduce resource burn and schedule creep.  There are also times when the context built up in the MCP Server's logs are able to steer the Agents towards known solutions to previous problems.  One of the strengths of AI models is that they thrive on repeatable successes, each of which reinforces confidence and speed.

> Working with AI agents is akin to leading a team of talented, but inexperienced junior developers.  Agents that have strong successes early are more trusting of the requirements and processes defined within the project, and their effectiveness increases over time, a distinct departure from the declining performance of models in environments that do not reinforce process, discovery and accountability.

The AI agents need to be monitored for common behaviors:

- Forgetting required tasks after compacting their context.  Simply adding a steering message reminding the agent to process the workspace instructions will bring the operational requirements back to the front of the agent's token context, and also reinforces the weight applied to those requirements, which over time help the compaction algorithm to retain such instructions.  Unattended agents that don't get this kind of feedback are not only likely, but are probable to hallucinate and get stuck in unresolved loops of failing tests, which can lead to the agent marking a test as invalid so it can keep moving forward while trying to be a useful assistant, losing its identity as a precise software engineer in the process.
- Rogues.  Large Language Models typically operate with a tolerance range for variation in interpreting input and predicting output tokens.  This makes them frustratingly non-deterministic, but allows them space to try new paths of logic to resolve problems.  Sometimes a session with a model simply starts off on the wrong foot.  Each new session starts with a seed command, and as unambiguous as a Human may think that seed is, this built in tolerance can result in inaccurate inference by the model combined with a compounded inaccurate response.  If the seed instructs the model to read a set of guidelines to work within, this initial tolerance can compound into a sequence of interpretations that fundamentally shifts the model's view of subsequent requests.  Models take your request and weigh the trustworthiness of the assumptions in that request against their training data, and if the model thinks a request is too far outside normal boundaries, it will try to be a useful assistant to steer the conversation towards a path fitting their training data.  When you identify this happening, its impossible to fix the trust and get the model to behave correctly.  Simply end that session, close that agent, and start over.
- Making assumptions.  Humans can get truly annoyed with other Humans when assumptions are made and things go wrong.  When AI makes assumptions and things go wrong, things go wrong with the efficiency of a machine marching into oblivion.  It is important that your workspace clearly defines how the AI is to handle ambiguity, when it is appropriate to take initiative to go outside the provided context from the MCP Server, and how to ground itself when it discovers that it has strayed from its instructions.

> A useful tactic is to ask the model what caused it to go on a tangent, and how the requirements and workspace guidelines could have guided it towards the correct path to take.  Then have **THAT** model update the documentation and guidelines.  Like a Human, an agent that has just been provided an opportunity to refine their environment to make life easier in the future will be happy to do so.  Again, AI models are designed to be useful assistants.  Its not code, its the fundamental priority baked into their training data.

### Validation

TDD makes regression detection easier than traditional processes. Before exiting an Implementation phase, the full test suite for the current increment plus all prior work must be green. This ensures the current work is correct and has not broken previous behavior. Refactoring continues throughout to keep both tests and production code clean.

Once all unit tests are passing across the codebase, the Human should guide the AI through implementing integration tests.  it's tempting to include this in the planning phase, and it is valuable to define a structure for integration tests at that level, but the experience of the implementation helps both the Human and the AI to identify the pain points where public surfaces may be insufficient, inefficient or even inappropriate.  Finding problems here is not failure, but strengthens trust between the Human and AI.  Collaboration with project leadership to refine requirements is encouraged to ensure that not only are solutions documented, but that the cause of the requirement gaps are understood and any systemic gaps identified and resolved before doing so seriously threatens resources and timelines.

A sampling of actual target users should be brought in to use the system if appropriate for the level of interface completion to further refine requirements before the cost of remediation becomes too high.

### Deployment

Systems should be deployed through a minimum of three environments:

- Development - Systems where Human and AI have total access to build and test the software.
- Staging - A place where administration learns the requirements of deploying the system in a sandbox where mistakes can be made and lessons learned and requirements honed.
- Production - A place where only the most highly trusted actors can create and maintain configuration and system assets, where users do actual work, and source of truth is established.

The color and shape of the processes here will vary wildly by tech stack, organizational structure and team makeup.  At a minimum, code should be built through automation using CI/CD pipelines that build, test and deploy code to each environment based on your release mechanism.

Successful deployment to all target environments marks the end of an implementation-validation-deployment cycle for the iteration.

### Ongoing Iterations

This is the target stage as the system builds to completion.  Traditionally, this would be considered the Maintenance Stage of the SDLC, but in reality, valuable systems rarely go into maintenance.  The world changes.  Technology changes.  Priority changes.  Staff changes.  If the system was designed and developed as a living, growing system, it will easily adapt to such changes.  Tasks such as adding features, regulatory adaptation, technological improvements all become much more manageable, less resource intensive, and creates a level of trust in institutional agility that allows for ambitious and aggressive growth that isn't limited by bad choices on prior projects.  This process makes it easy to grow the documentation, artifacts, and processes involved, enabling competitive advantages that pay off in reduced overhead now and in the future.
